API reference

The package defines a single module OracleD. Docstrings are spliced in below; every entry corresponds to a public binding of the module. The module does not export anything, so these names are accessed as OracleD.<name>.

Entry point

OracleD.main — Function
main() -> Simulation

Entry point of the baseline simulation, the counterpart of the Python src/Main.py script: read config.json from the repository root, load the cluster inventory, create the run directory and logger, then build and run the Simulation.

Simulation and main loop

OracleD.Simulation — Type
Simulation

Owns the full simulation state: the clock, the carbon intensity data, the cluster, the job scheduler and the data logger. Constructing a Simulation performs all setup (including seeding the initial jobs) and prints the setup banner; start! then runs the main loop to completion.

OracleD.start! — Function
start!(simulation)

Run the simulation main loop until either all jobs have completed or the configured maximum simulated duration has passed, then print the summary.

OracleD._load_carbon_intensity_data — Function
_load_carbon_intensity_data(path, datastart_str, datafinal_str)
    -> Vector{CarbonIntensityEntry}

Read the carbon intensity CSV, keeping the rows from the one whose datetime matches datastart_str up to (but excluding) the one matching datafinal_str. Rows with missing forecast or actual values produce the same console warnings as the Python code (and are stored as NaN).

Time

OracleD.SimulationTime — Type
SimulationTime

The shared simulated clock.

Fields:

  • time: the current simulated DateTime.
  • start_time: the simulated DateTime the run started from.
  • timestep_seconds: how far advance! moves the clock each step.
  • origin: the real (wall-clock) DateTime the simulation was created at.
  • verbosity: the configured output verbosity, used to gate log messages.
OracleD.set_to_current_time! — Function
set_to_current_time!(simulation_time)

Set the simulated clock to the current wall-clock time, truncated to the minute (as the Python code does by round-tripping through a string).

OracleD.set_to_time! — Function
set_to_time!(simulation_time, time::DateTime)

Set the simulated clock to time.

OracleD.find_hh_segment — Function
find_hh_segment(simulation_time, dt, instruction = "current") -> DateTime

Find the half-hour segment boundary associated with dt. With instruction == "current" this is the boundary at or before dt; with instruction == "next" it is the boundary strictly after dt (a dt exactly on a boundary counts as belonging to the previous segment).

OracleD.advance! — Function
advance!(simulation_time)

Move the simulated clock forward by one timestep.

OracleD.get_start_datetime — Function
get_start_datetime(simulation_time) -> DateTime

Get the simulated start time of the run.

OracleD.get_origin_datetime — Function
get_origin_datetime(simulation_time) -> DateTime

Get the real (wall-clock) time the simulation was started at.

OracleD.get_current_datetime — Function
get_current_datetime(simulation_time) -> DateTime

Get the current simulated time.

OracleD.get_timestep — Function
get_timestep(simulation_time) -> Int

Get the simulation timestep in seconds.

Jobs

OracleD.Job — Type
Job

A single unit of work submitted to the cluster.

Fields:

  • name: unique job name, e.g. "ATLAS-Prod-17".
  • duration: the job length in seconds (scaled by node performance when the job starts).
  • memory_req: requested memory in GB per core.
  • cores_req: number of cores (threads) requested.
  • start_time / end_time: simulated schedule of the job, UNSET_TIME until the job has been started. Use set_duration!, set_start_time! and set_end_time! to keep them consistent.
OracleD.set_duration! — Function
set_duration!(job, value)

Set the job duration in seconds. If the job has already started, its end time is recomputed from the start time and the new duration.

OracleD.set_start_time! — Function
set_start_time!(job, value::DateTime)

Set the job start time; the end time is derived from the current duration.

OracleD.set_end_time! — Function
set_end_time!(job, value::DateTime)

Directly set the job end time, for processes that change the life of a job while it is in progress (e.g. clocking a node up or down).

VO job factories

OracleD.AbstractVOJobFactory — Type
AbstractVOJobFactory

Common supertype of the per-VO job factories. Each concrete factory stores the same state (tag, running job number, memory per core and the cached core request) and specialises get_duration and require_cores!.

Note

As in the Python original, the number of cores drawn for the first job is cached in cores_requested and reused for every subsequent job from the same factory. This quirk is preserved deliberately so the Julia simulation reproduces the Python results.

OracleD.VOJobFactory — Type
VOJobFactory(tag, RAM_per_core = 1, cores_req = 0) -> VOJobFactory

Basic VO job factory producing short "empty pilot" jobs of ~15 minutes, with a 50% chance that all its jobs require 8 cores rather than 1. A cores_req of 0 means "not yet decided" (Python None).

OracleD.GridPPJobFactory — Type
GridPPJobFactory(tag, RAM_per_core = 2, cores_req = 0) -> GridPPJobFactory

Test VO factory that fixes all job variables: every job runs for exactly 5 hours on a single core (unless cores_req is given).

OracleD.ATLASJobFactory — Type
ATLASJobFactory(tag, RAM_per_core = 2, cores_req = 0) -> ATLASJobFactory

ATLAS production job factory: ~42% short pilot jobs (~15 min), otherwise ~5 hour jobs; ~80% chance the factory produces 8-core jobs.

OracleD.LHCbJobFactory — Type
LHCbJobFactory(tag, RAM_per_core = 4, cores_req = 0) -> LHCbJobFactory

LHCb production job factory: ~22% short pilot jobs, otherwise job lengths drawn from a Landau-like distribution between 9.5 and 18.5 hours; ~10% chance the factory produces 8-core jobs.

OracleD.get_duration — Function
get_duration(factory) -> Float64

Sample a job duration in seconds for a job from factory.

OracleD.require_cores! — Function
require_cores!(factory) -> Int

Return the number of cores jobs from this factory request. On the first call (when cores_requested == 0) the value is drawn randomly according to the VO's multi-core probability and cached for all later jobs.

OracleD.debug_label — Function
debug_label(factory) -> String

The debug-log message emitted when factory creates a job.

OracleD.create_job! — Function
create_job!(factory) -> Job

Create the next Job from factory, advancing its job counter.

Cluster and worker nodes

OracleD.WorkerNodeSpec — Type
WorkerNodeSpec

Immutable description of one machine type in the cluster inventory, the Julia counterpart of the dynamically generated Python WorkerNode subclasses.

Fields:

  • node_key: name of the machine type, e.g. "DESYT3_0"; used as the hostname prefix of instantiated nodes.
  • threads: number of (hyper)threads per machine.
  • memory_gb: RAM per machine in GB.
  • idle_power_w: average instantaneous power dissipated by an idle node in W.
  • frequencies: available CPU frequencies in GHz, sorted descending (the first entry is the default maximum).
  • powers_w: average instantaneous power dissipated in W by a fully occupied node at each frequency.
  • hepscores: HEPScore23 benchmark score at each frequency.
  • system, cpu_model, install_year: descriptive metadata.
OracleD.WorkerNode — Type
WorkerNode

A simulated worker node.

Power-related quantities are stored as energy use per second (the W values from the specification divided by 3600, as in the Python code). Job durations are rescaled when jobs start according to the node's HEPScore relative to the reference machine (see fixed_duration_multiplier), and again when the node is clocked up or down (dynamic_duration_multiplier).

OracleD.number_of_cores — Function
number_of_cores(worker_node) -> Int

Number of job slots on the node. As in the Python original this is the number of threads (people interchange cores with threads when counting job slots); the physical-core count used for power scaling is the physical_cores field.

OracleD.is_awaiting_jobs — Function
is_awaiting_jobs(worker_node) -> Bool

Whether the node has at least one free core.

OracleD.get_free_core_count — Function
get_free_core_count(worker_node) -> Int

Number of currently unoccupied cores (threads) on the node.

OracleD.get_memory_available — Function
get_memory_available(worker_node) -> Float64

Amount of currently unallocated RAM on the node in GB.

OracleD.can_schedule_job — Function
can_schedule_job(worker_node, job) -> Bool

Whether job fits on the node right now. Note that, as in the Python original, only the per-core memory request is checked against the free memory (not memory_req * cores_req).

OracleD.set_running_frequency! — Function
set_running_frequency!(worker_node, value)

Set the node's running frequency, recording the previous one. Throws an error if value is not one of the node's available frequencies.

OracleD.start_job! — Function
start_job!(worker_node, job)

Start job on the node: stamp its start time, rescale its sampled duration by the node's performance (fixed multiplier and current-frequency HEPScore) and allocate cores and memory.

OracleD.timestep_power_dissipated — Function
timestep_power_dissipated(worker_node) -> Float64

The amount of energy used by the machine in one timestep, in kWh. Machines always draw at least the idle power; above that, power scales linearly with the number of busy physical cores up to the fully-active power.

OracleD.change_clock_speed! — Function
change_clock_speed!(worker_node, clockspeed)

Change the clock frequency of the node to clockspeed (GHz) and rescale the remaining time of every running job by the current dynamic duration multiplier.

OracleD.clock_down! — Function
clock_down!(worker_node)

Decrease the frequency of the node by one available frequency step, adjusting its active power draw and stretching running jobs by the ratio of HEPScores. Prints a message if the node is already at its lowest frequency.

OracleD.clock_up! — Function
clock_up!(worker_node)

Increase the frequency of the node by one available frequency step, adjusting its active power draw and shrinking running jobs by the ratio of HEPScores. Prints a message if the node is already at its maximum frequency.

OracleD.update! — Function
update!(worker_node)

Advance the node by one timestep: finish any jobs whose end time has been reached, freeing their cores and memory and reporting them to the data logger.

The recorded duration of a finished job reproduces Python's timedelta.seconds, i.e. the whole-seconds part of the elapsed time with full days discarded.

update!(cluster)

Advance the cluster by one timestep: update all nodes, try to schedule queued jobs, apply the configured energy-saving policy, and report the timestep's energy, carbon and occupancy to the data logger. Sets mission_accomplished when no jobs are running or queued.

update!(scheduler)

Submit any regular incoming job batches whose cycle boundary coincides with the current simulated time. Nothing is submitted while the cluster is completely idle with an empty queue (the run is about to end).

OracleD.CarbonIntensityEntry — Type
CarbonIntensityEntry

One record of grid carbon intensity data: the start of a data segment, the forecast intensity and the actual intensity (both in gCO2e/kWh).

OracleD.Cluster — Type
Cluster

The cluster to be simulated: a set of worker nodes, the queue of jobs waiting to be scheduled, and the state needed to apply the configured energy-saving policy against the grid carbon intensity data.

OracleD.get_number_of_nodes — Function
get_number_of_nodes(cluster) -> Int

Total number of worker nodes in the cluster.

OracleD.get_number_of_cores — Function
get_number_of_cores(cluster) -> Int

Total number of job slots (threads) across all worker nodes.

OracleD.submit_job! — Function
submit_job!(cluster, job)

Add job to the cluster's queue and notify the data logger.

OracleD.has_queued_jobs — Function
has_queued_jobs(cluster) -> Bool

Whether any jobs are waiting in the queue.

OracleD.has_running_jobs — Function
has_running_jobs(cluster) -> Bool

Whether any worker node is currently running jobs.

OracleD.cluster_occupancy — Function
cluster_occupancy(cluster) -> Float64

The fraction of all job slots that are currently busy.

Cluster loading

OracleD.load_frequency_map — Function
load_frequency_map(frequency_csv, strict = true)
    -> Dict{String,Dict{Float64,Tuple{Float64,Float64}}}

Load the per-node-type frequency dependence map from CSV. Each entry maps a node key (type_subtype) to a dictionary of frequency GHz => (power W, HEPScore).

With strict = true malformed entries raise an error; otherwise they are logged and skipped.

OracleD.load_cluster_inventory — Function
load_cluster_inventory(machinegroups_inventory_csv, frequency_dependence_csv;
                       cluster_name = nothing, strict = true)
    -> Vector{Tuple{WorkerNodeSpec,Int}}

Load the cluster inventory as an ordered list of (machine type specification, quantity) pairs — the Julia counterpart of the Python {WorkerNodeSubclass: quantity} mapping, preserving the CSV row order.

Arguments

  • machinegroups_inventory_csv: path to the machine inventory CSV.
  • frequency_dependence_csv: path to the frequency dependence CSV.
  • cluster_name: optional filter on the cluster(main_Puppet_hostgroup) column.
  • strict: if true, raise on malformed or missing data; if false, log a warning and skip the offending row.

Job scheduler

OracleD.JobScheduler — Type
JobScheduler

Seeds the cluster with an initial mix of jobs at construction and, if configured, submits further job batches at regular simulated intervals.

initial_job_mix maps VO names ("ATLAS", "LHCb", "GridPP", anything else is a basic VO job) to job counts. regular_incoming_jobs is a list of (job mix, cycle length in seconds) pairs; an empty list means no regular submissions.

Data logger

OracleD.DataLogger — Type
DataLogger

Accumulates run statistics (job counts, CPU time, energy, carbon and occupancy) and produces the end-of-run summary on the console and in the run directory (summary.txt and summary.json).

OracleD.job_start! — Function
job_start!(datalogger, job, worker_node)

Record that job has started on worker_node.

OracleD.job_finish! — Function
job_finish!(datalogger, job, worker_node)

Record that job has finished on worker_node, accumulating its wallclock and CPU time.

OracleD.energy_and_carbon_consumed! — Function
energy_and_carbon_consumed!(datalogger, timestep_energy_consumed, timestep_carbon_consumed_per_unit_energy)

Accumulate the energy dissipated in a timestep (kWh) and the corresponding carbon (energy times the grid carbon intensity in g/kWh).

OracleD.peaktime_energy_and_carbon_consumed! — Function
peaktime_energy_and_carbon_consumed!(datalogger, timestep_energy_consumed, timestep_carbon_consumed_per_unit_energy)

As energy_and_carbon_consumed! but accumulated into the peak-time (5pm-9pm) totals.

OracleD.sum_occupancy! — Function
sum_occupancy!(datalogger, timestep_occupancy)

Accumulate the cluster occupancy fraction for one timestep (divided by the number of timesteps when the simulation ends to give the average).

OracleD.print_summary — Function
print_summary(datalogger, summary_file, additional_description,
              total_simulated_time, timestepinsec, total_real_time)

Compute the derived averages, print the run summary to the console and, when summary_file is true, append it to summary.txt and write the machine-readable summary.json in the run directory.

Logging

OracleD.SimLogger — Type
SimLogger

A minimal file logger for the simulation, playing the role of the Python logging logger named CLUSTERSIM.

Until configure_logger! is called the logger is unconfigured and all messages are dropped (just as the Python logger has no handler before configure_logger() runs). Afterwards messages are appended to simulation.log in the run directory.

OracleD.get_logger — Function
get_logger() -> SimLogger

Return the shared simulation logger, mirroring the Python Logging.get_logger() helper.

OracleD.configure_logger! — Function
configure_logger!(logger::SimLogger, debug::Bool, run_dir::AbstractString)

Point logger at <run_dir>/simulation.log and set whether debug messages are recorded. Any previously opened log file is closed first.

OracleD.close_logger! — Function
close_logger!(logger::SimLogger)

Close the log file (if open) and return the logger to its unconfigured state.

OracleD.log_info — Function
log_info(logger::SimLogger, message)

Record an INFO-level message. Dropped if the logger is not yet configured.

OracleD.log_warning — Function
log_warning(logger::SimLogger, message)

Record a WARNING-level message. Dropped if the logger is not yet configured.

OracleD.log_debug — Function
log_debug(logger::SimLogger, message)

Record a DEBUG-level message. Only written when the logger was configured with debug = true.

OracleD.normalize_verbosity — Function
normalize_verbosity(raw_verbosity, default = "high") -> String

Map the configured verbosity onto one of ("low", "medium", "high"), returning default when the value is missing or invalid.

OracleD.default_run_label — Function
default_run_label(config) -> String

Build the fallback run label <total initial jobs>jobs_<savings policy> used when output.run_label is not present in the configuration.

OracleD.slugify — Function
slugify(value) -> String

Reduce value to a lower-case filesystem-friendly slug: runs of non-alphanumeric characters become _, leading/trailing _ are stripped, and an empty result becomes "simulation".

OracleD.create_run_directory — Function
create_run_directory(config) -> String

Create a unique per-run output directory named <timestamp>_<run label slug> below output.log_dir (default logs/runs), store it in config["output"]["run_dir"] and return it.

Utilities

OracleD.project_root — Function
project_root() -> String

Return the absolute path of the ORACLE-D repository root, i.e. the parent directory of the OracleD.jl package directory.

All relative paths found in config.json (data files, log directories) are resolved against this directory, so the simulation behaves the same regardless of the current working directory.

OracleD.resolve_path — Function
resolve_path(path) -> String

Resolve path against project_root unless it is already absolute.

OracleD.weighted_choice — Function
weighted_choice(values, probabilities) -> eltype(values)

Draw a single random element from values with the given (normalised) probabilities. This is the equivalent of the Python numpy.random.choice(values, p=probabilities) call used to model the LHCb job-length distribution.

OracleD.gauss — Function
gauss(mu, sigma) -> Float64

Sample from a normal distribution with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, mirroring Python's random.gauss(mu, sigma).

OracleD.pystr — Function
pystr(dt::DateTime) -> String

Format a DateTime the way Python's str(datetime) does, e.g. "2024-01-16 16:00:00". Milliseconds are included only when non-zero.

OracleD.pynum — Function
pynum(x) -> String

Format a number the way Python's string interpolation would: integers without a decimal point, everything else via string. Used where the Python code prints values taken straight from config.json.

OracleD.total_seconds — Function
total_seconds(period) -> Float64

Return the total number of seconds in a Dates period difference between two DateTimes, mirroring Python's timedelta.total_seconds().
